title: The cost of solving the wrong problem
summary: Discover why focusing solely on cost reduction and efficiency can undermine customer outcomes, and how to improve customer operations by solving the right problems.
body_markdown:
I’ve spent much of my career working with organisations looking to improve customer operations. The conversations often start in the same old territory: the share price is underperforming or our cost/income ratio isn’t good enough.


Ultimately this leads to all-too-familiar questions like, ‘How can we reduce costs?’, ‘Can we automate more?’, ‘Should we change the sourcing model?’, ‘Could this be delivered from a different location?


They’re all valid questions. In many cases answering them can deliver value. The danger comes when an organisation becomes so focused on improving one particular metric e.g. cost, that it loses sight of the actual problem it was trying to resolve.


And when that happens – particularly when decisions become overly-focused on financial metrics – the eventual improvements don’t always feel like improvements.


The constant pressure to become more efficient is understandable. Leaders want to reduce costs, improve productivity and make better use of resources. So attention often turns to things like AHT (average handling time), cost per interaction or automation levels. All of this is perfectly sensible.


The problem is that customers don’t experience metrics: they deal with outcomes. A customer doesn’t care whether an interaction lasted three minutes or six. They care whether their problem was solved.


Here’s some of what they care about. Did they hear the answer they needed? Did they get transferred between different teams? Did they end up having to call back?


I’ve sat in plenty of discussions (perhaps you have too) where teams might spend months debating how work should be organised, where it should sit and who should perform it. All reasonable decisions, but far less time is spent discussing what a successful outcome actually looks like from the customer’s perspective.


Once you start looking at this, different questions are asked.


- What task is the customer trying to achieve?
- Where are we making that task harder than it needs to be?
- Which journeys have the biggest impact on trust?
- Where does human judgement matter most?
- What would make this experience genuinely easier?
- Where is a regulator likely to address poor outcomes?


I’ve been in organisations that significantly reduce the cost of handling an interaction, only to create additional contacts, rework and escalation elsewhere, which ended up also bringing a regulatory focus and all the attendant costs that brings.


On paper, one metric improves, but in reality, the customer ends up doing more work and so does the business. The problem hasn’t been solved, it’s just been shifted somewhere else.


This becomes particularly obvious when dealing with significant moments like fraud, financial difficulty or a bereavement. In situations like these, customers need more than an answer. They need clarity, accountability and the confidence that somebody understands their situation, and can help them get through whatever comes next.


Designing those experiences requires a different approach than simply asking how they can be delivered more efficiently. Yes, costs still matter. But each organisation needs to balance commercial reality with customer needs, regulatory compliance, skillset availability and so on…


When we stop focusing on the mechanics of delivery and start focusing on the outcome we’re trying to create, that’s when the most valuable discussions happen.


When you solve the right problem, decisions about operating models, sourcing and location become a lot clearer. So, before the next conversation about productivity, efficiency or cost reduction, I think it’s worth asking one simple question:


*Are we improving the metric, or the outcome?*


The answer often tells us whether we’re solving the right problem in the first place.
